passages.source_text: τούτου γὰρ ἕνεκεν ἀπὸ μὲν Ἑβραίων τὸν Μωϋσῆν διδάσκαλον εἰληφότων καλύπτεται ὁ Ἰησοῦς, ἀπὸ δὲ τῶν Ἰησοῦ πεπιστευκότων ὁ Μωϋσῆς ἀποκρύπτεται· μιᾶς γὰρ δι’ ἀμφοτέρων διδασκαλίας οὔσης τὸν τούτων τινὶ πεπιστευκότα ὁ θεὸς ἀποδέχεται. ἀλλὰ τὸ πιστεύειν διδασκάλῳ ἕνεκα τοῦ ποιεῖν τὰ ὑπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ λεγόμενα γίνεται. ὅτι δὲ τοῦθ’ οὕτως ἔχει, αὐτὸς ὁ κύριος ἡμῶν λέγει „ἐξομολογοῦμαί σοι, πάτερ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ καὶ τῆς γῆς, ὅτι ἔκρυψας ταῦτα ἀπὸ σοφῶν πρεσβυτέρων καὶ ἀπεκάλυψας αὐτὰ νηπίοις θηλάζουσιν“. οὕτως αὐτὸς ὁ θεὸς τοῖς μὲν ἔκρυψεν διδάσκαλον ὡς προεγνωκόσιν ἃ δεῖ πράττειν, τοῖς δὲ ἀπεκάλυψεν ὡς ἀγνοοῦσιν ἃ χρὴ ποιεῖν.

οὔτε οὖν Ἑβραῖοι περὶ ἀγνοίας Ἰησοῦ καταδικάζονται διὰ τὸν κρύψαντα, ἐάν γε πράττοντες τὰ διὰ Μωϋσέως .... ὃν ἠγνόησαν μὴ μισήσωσιν — οὔτ’ αὖ οἱ ἀπὸ ἐθνῶν ἀγνοήσαντες τὸν Μωϋσῆν διὰ τὸν καλύψαντα καταδικάζονται, ἐάνπερ καὶ οὗτοι πράσσοντες τὰ διὰ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ ῥηθέντα μὴ μισήσωσιν ὃν ἠγνόησαν. καὶ οὐκ ἐν τῷ τοὺς διδασκάλους κυρίους καλεῖν, τὰ δὲ δούλων μὴ ποιεῖν ὠφελοῦνταί τινες. τούτου γὰρ ἕνεκεν ὁ Ἰησοῦς ἡμῶν πρὸς τινὰ πυκνότερον κύριον αὐτὸν λέγοντα, μηδὲν δὲ ποιοῦντα ὧν αὐτὸς προσέτασσεν ἔφη „τί με λέγεις Κύριε κύριε καὶ οὐ ποιεῖς ἃ λέγω;“ οὐ γὰρ ὠφελήσει τινὰ τὸ λέγειν, ἀλλὰ τὸ ποιεῖν. ἐκ παντὸς οὖν τρόπου καλῶν ἔργων χρεία, πλὴν εἴ τις καταξιωθείη τοὺς ἀμφοτέρους ἐπιγνῶναι ὡς μιᾶς διδασκαλίας ὑπ’ αὐτῶν κεκηρυγμένης, οὗτος ἀνὴρ ἐν θεῷ πλούσιος κατηρίθμηται, τά τε ἀρχαῖα νέα τῷ χρόνῳ καὶ τὰ καινὰ παλαιὰ ὄντα νενοηκώς.

ταῦτα τοῦ Πέτρου λέγοντος, οἱ ὄχλοι ὥσπερ ὑπὸ τινὸς κληθέντες εἰσῄεσαν ἔνθα ὁ Πέτρος ἦν. ὁ δὲ τὸν πολὺν ὄχλον ἰδὼν ὥσπερ ποταμοῦ ἥσυχον ῥεῦμα πράως προσρέοντα, ἔφη τῷ Μαροόνῃ Ποῦ σοι τόπος ἐνταῦθα μᾶλλον τοὺς ὄχλους χωρεῖν δυνάμενος; τοῦ δὲ Μαροόνου εἰς τόπον ὕπαιθρον κεκηπευμένον προάγοντος αὐτόν, εἵποντο οἱ ὄχλοι. ὁ δὲ Πέτρος ἐπὶ τινὸς βάσεως ἀνδριάντος οὐ πάνυ ὑψηλῆς ἐπιστάς, ἅμα τῷ τὸν ὄχλον θεοσεβεῖ ἔθει προσαγορεῦσαι, εἰδὼς πολλοὺς ἐκ τῶν παρεστώτων ὄχλων ὑπὸ δαιμόνων τε καὶ πολλῶν παθῶν ἐκ πολλῶν χρόνων ἐνοχλουμένους, βρύχοντάς τε μετὰ οἰμωγῆς καὶ πίπτοντας μεθ᾽ ἱκεσίας, ἐπιτιμήσας αὐτοῖς καὶ ἡσυχίαν ἔχειν προστάξας καὶ τὴν ἴασιν μετὰ τὸ διαλεχθῆναι ὑποσχόμενος τοῦ λέγειν ἤρξατο οὕτως·

Ἀρχόμενος τὸν ὑπὲρ θεοσεβείας λόγον ποιεῖσθαι τοῖς παντελῶς ἀγνοοῦσι τὰ πάντα καὶ ὑπὸ τῶν τοῦ ἀντικειμένου ἡμῖν Σίμωνος διαβολῶν ἐσπιλωμένοις τὸν νοῦν, ἀναγκαῖον ἡγησάμην πρῶτον ὑπὲρ τοῦ μὴ δεῖν μέμφεσθαι τὸν τὰ πάντα πεποιηκότα θεὸν τὸν λόγον ποιήσασθαι, οὐκ ἄλλοθεν ἀρχόμενος ἢ ἀπ᾽ αὐτῆς τῆς κατὰ πρόνοιαν ὑπ᾽ αὐτοῦ εὐκαίρως ὑποβληθείσης προφάσεως, ἵνα γνωσθῇ ὡς εὐλόγως οἱ πολλοὶ ὑπὸ πολλῶν δαιμόνων συνεσχέθησαν καὶ ὑπὸ ἀλλοκότων παθῶν κατελήφθησαν, ὅπως καὶ ἐν τούτῳ τὸ τοῦ θεοῦ δίκαιον φανῇ. καὶ οἱ δι᾽ ἄγνοιαν μεμφόμενοι αὐτὸν κἂν νῦν μαθόντες ὡς δεῖ φρονεῖν, δι᾽ εὐφημίας τε καὶ εὐποιΐας τοῦ προτέρου ἐγκλήματος ἑαυτοὺς ἀνακαλέσωνται, αἰτίαν τοῦ κακοῦ τολμήματος τὴν ἄγνοιαν εἰς τὴν συγγνώμην προθέμενοι.

ἔχει δὲ οὕτως· τοῦ μόνου ἀγαθοῦ θεοῦ τὰ πάντα καλῶς πεποιηκότος καὶ παραδεδωκότος τῷ κατ᾽ εἰκόνα αὐτοῦ γενομένῳ ἀνθρώπῳ, ὁ γεγονὼς τῆς τοῦ πεποιηκότος αὐτὸν πνέων θειότητος, ἀληθὴς προφήτης ὢν καὶ εἰδὼς τὰ ὅλα, εἰς τιμὴν τοῦ πάντα αὐτῷ δωρησαμένου πατρὸς καὶ εἰς σωτηρίαν τῶν ἐξ αὐτοῦ γενομένων υἱῶν, ὡς πατὴρ γνήσιος πρὸς τοὺς ὑπ᾽ αὐτοῦ γενομένους παῖδας ἀποσώζων τὸ εὔνουν, βουλόμενος αὐτοὺς πρὸς τὸ συμφέρον αὐτοῖς φιλεῖν θεὸν καὶ φιλεῖσθαι ὑπ᾽ αὐτοῦ, τὴν πρὸς φιλίαν αὐτοῦ ἄγουσαν ἐξέφηνεν ὁδόν, διδάξας ποίαις ἀνθρώπων πράξεσιν ὁ μόνος καὶ πάντων δεσπότης θεὸς εὐφραίνεται, καὶ τὰ ἐκείνῳ δοκοῦντα ἐκφήνας νόμον αἰώνιον ὥρισεν τοῖς ὅλοις, μήτε πολέμῳ ἐμπρησθῆναι δυνάμενον μήθ᾽ ὑπὸ ἀσεβοῦς τινὸς ὑπονοθευόμενον μήτε ἐνὶ τόπῳ ἀποκεκρυμμένον, ἀλλὰ πᾶσιν ἀναγνωσθῆναι δυνάμενον. ἦν οὖν αὐτοῖς ἐκ τῆς πειθαρχίας τοῦ νόμου πάντα ἄφθονα, τὰ τῶν καρπῶν κάλλιστα, τὰ τῶν ἐτῶν τέλεια καὶ ἄλυπα καὶ ἄνοσα, μετὰ πάσης τῆς τῶν ἀέρων εὐκρασίας ἀδεῶς δεδωρημένα.

context.translation_policy_text:
# Translation Stance

This document states the translation commitments that guide every
decision in the People's Open Bible. Declaring them is an act of
honesty: critics can assess our output against our stated
commitments rather than guessing at hidden biases.

> **Status: first draft.** This document will be refined as the
> project matures. Input and disagreement are welcomed via GitHub
> issues.

## Theological stance

The People's Open Bible does not commit to a specific denominational
or creedal doctrinal stance. Where the source texts presuppose
theological claims — the divinity of Christ, the resurrection,
the personhood of the Holy Spirit, the unity of God — the
translation reflects those claims as the texts present them, not
as imposed commitments of the translator.

Readers from any tradition (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant
of any stripe, non-denominational, inquirer) are invited to
evaluate POB against their own framework. Where a translation
decision is influenced by a theological reading — for example,
where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

4. **Consistency of key terms, or documented exception.** A given
   Greek or Hebrew word should receive a consistent English gloss
   across the translation, unless context demands variance — in
   which case the variance is documented per-verse with a
   rationale. The `consistency_lint.py` tool enforces this at
   commit time.

5. **Readable modern English, not archaic or academic.** The
   target reader is a literate 18–35-year-old English speaker.
   Vocabulary should be accessible without flattening theological
   weight. We avoid both ecclesiastical jargon ("propitiation" is
   footnoted, not required) and informality that undersells the
   text's gravity.

## Source distinctions and optimal English

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for
maintainer review; do not silently certify them as unchanged or auto-publish.

**Approved scoped rendering:** John 21:15–17 uses **agape-love** for ἀγαπάω
and **phileo-love** for φιλέω, including the repeated question in verse 17.
The ἀγάπη noun's general table entry below is not a rule erasing that verb
pattern. Do not revert this approved POB/SPOB wording to generic “love”.

## Contested terms

The following terms appear frequently and carry heavy theological
weight. Our default rendering and rationale are recorded here.
Per-verse variance is documented in the individual YAML files.

| Greek / Hebrew | Default English | Alternatives considered | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| Χριστός *Christos* | Messiah where independently titular; Christ in the name forms "Jesus Christ" / "Christ Jesus" | Christ, Messiah | Preserves the title's Hebraic messianic meaning while using the recognizable conventional English personal name |
| κύριος *Kyrios* | Lord | LORD, Master | Matches covenantal and NT usage |
| δοῦλος *doulos* | servant | bondservant, slave | Uses reader-facing "servant" consistently; documents bonded-status and ownership nuance in notes/audit metadata |
| πίστις *pistis* | faith | faithfulness, trust | Main text: faith; footnote alternatives where contested |
| δικαιοσύνη *dikaiosynē* | righteousness | justice | Both renderings preserved in footnotes for Pauline passages |
| ἱλαστήριον *hilastērion* | atoning sacrifice | propitiation, mercy seat | Dynamic rendering for accessibility; alternatives footnoted |
| ἀγάπη *agapē* | love | charity (archaic) | Lexical cognates in source kept |
| σάρξ *sarx* | flesh (literal) / sinful nature (metaphorical) | — | Context-dependent; per-verse documented |
| μετανοέω / μετάνοια *metanoeō / metanoia* | reorient / reorientation; toward God where the context warrants making the destination explicit | repent / repentance (traditional); reconsider / change of mind in documented exceptions | See "Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)" below; do not homogenize regret, divine relenting, or distinct turning words |
| νήφω *nēphō* | clear-minded (most contexts); sober (where Paul explicitly runs the drunk/sober metaphor) | sober-minded | See revision notes in 1 Pet 5:8, 1 Thess 5:6 |
| יְהוָה YHWH | Yahweh | the LORD, Jehovah | Renders the divine name as a name. Where the NT quotes an OT YHWH passage using *Kyrios*, the NT verse retains "Lord" to preserve the Greek; the OT source verse uses "Yahweh". |
| אָדָם *adam* | man / humankind (context) | — | Context-dependent per usage |

## Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)

Maintainer-approved English POB and SPOB reader wording uses **reorient /
reorientation** in place of the repent family for moral-spiritual redirection.
Use **toward God** when the context warrants making that direction explicit;
use **toward you** in direct prayer, and omit the extra destination when the
sentence already names it, supplies a departure from wrongdoing, or concerns
interpersonal reconsideration. Acts 20:21 explicitly supplies the Godward
phrase. The word *metanoia* by itself does not lexically contain "God."

This is an English editorial policy, not a claim that remorse is irrelevant or
that Greek word parts establish the full meaning. Preserve sorrow, named sins,
faith, forgiveness, and the distinction between a response and its fruit.
Keep separate turning expressions in Acts 3:19 and 26:20. Baptism's relationship
to reorientation must not be rewritten as "only symbolizes" or "causes."

**Context controls exceptions.** Retain regret, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where that is the supported sense. Do not make
God reorient toward God; do not make a persecutor's demand for apostasy a call
toward God. Preserve contested interpretations in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17.
Extra-canonical authors retain their own conceptual frameworks. Adapting a
historical English witness is not a new ancient-language translation, and must
be disclosed while its source transcription remains untouched.

**No invented intensifiers.** Do not add "fully," "completely," "radically,"
"truly," "wholeheartedly," or a superlative simply to strengthen reorientation.
Preserve such force only where the source supplies it. Hermas V.3.xiii.4
(reader chapter 21:4) has *holotelōs* and *ex holēs kardias*; its existing
"completely" and "from their whole heart" are not new additions.

Traditional terminology remains in alternative notes, original sources, and
historical revision records. Do not rewrite those layers to manufacture a
history of agreement. See [the application report](docs/REORIENTATION_POLICY_2026-10-11.md)
and the hash-bound plan in `config/terminology/`.

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.
- **Not a study Bible.** Footnotes document translation decisions,
  not doctrinal application or devotional commentary.
- **Not a denominational product.** The translation is
  intentionally cross-denominational. Contested readings are
  preserved in footnotes, not smoothed away.
- **Not a finalized translation.** Every verse is currently an
  AI-drafted rendering, released openly with full rationale. There
  is no formal scholarly review process at this time.
- **Not a first-century English approximation.** We aim at modern
  English that honors source-language meaning, not at archaism.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model
performance and feasibility.** Not every language has an AI model
capable of scholarly-accurate translation yet, and not every
language has a sufficient community of native-speaking reviewers
accessible to the project. We will publish the current supported-
language list, and the ready-but-not-yet-stable list, as we reach
the capability threshold for each. Languages that do not yet meet
the bar are named as such, not silently omitted.

Every language published under this program carries the same
CC-BY 4.0 license, the same per-verse provenance, the same
auditability. There is no tier system across languages — every
supported language gets the full People's Open Bible.

## Change log for this document

Material changes to this document are themselves commits. Prior
versions of the stance are preserved in git history.

- **2026-04-21:** Removed creedal affirmations (Apostles' Creed,
  Nicene Creed, Chalcedonian Definition) and replaced with a
  theological-stance section that declines specific creedal
  commitment. Translation philosophy and contested-terms table
  preserved unchanged; those are methodology, not creedal
  commitment, and the project actually runs on them. Added a
  "Translating into other languages" section stating POB's long-
  term intention to ship in every feasible major language, with
  the full revision pipeline and transparent supported-language
  disclosure. Per-verse YAML citing the old `doctrine_reference`
  values is preserved as historical record; those are not
  retroactively edited.
context.ambiguity_review_standard: Apply the supplied DOCTRINE.md ambiguity policy: a defensible contextual rendering may be used in the main text when material alternatives and the reason for the choice are preserved in notes. A unique or uncontested interpretation is not required. Distinguish (a) an unreadable or unverified source, omitted content, invented restoration, or a construction for which no defensible English can be given, from (b) ordinary lexical, attachment, or referent ambiguity faithfully preserved in English or explained with viable alternatives. The former blocks publication; the latter does not automatically block it. A note cannot excuse unsupported wording: the proposed main rendering must itself be defensible from the supplied Greek. Clearly printed gaps must remain gaps, not be filled by invention. Never change a verdict merely to achieve acceptance.

passages.text: For this reason, Jesus is concealed from the Hebrews who have received Moses as teacher, while Moses is hidden from those who have trusted Jesus; for since the teaching through both is one, God accepts the person who has trusted either of them. But trusting a teacher is for the sake of doing the things spoken by God. That this is so, our Lord himself says: “I praise you, Father of heaven and earth, because you hid these things from wise elders and revealed them to nursing infants.” Thus God himself hid a teacher from some, since they already knew what must be done, but revealed one to others, since they did not know what they ought to do.

lexical_decisions.chosen: those who have trusted Jesus
lexical_decisions.rationale: The perfect of πιστεύω with a personal object can denote placing trust in someone; “believed Jesus” is also possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: I praise you
lexical_decisions.rationale: In an address to God, ἐξομολογοῦμαι can express praise or thanksgiving rather than confession; “I give thanks to you” is a viable alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: wise elders
lexical_decisions.rationale: Both adjectives/nouns are retained as printed rather than harmonized with a familiar form of the quotation.

lexical_decisions.chosen: since they already knew
lexical_decisions.rationale: The context contrasts prior knowledge of what to do with ignorance; the more formally temporal “since they had known beforehand” remains possible.

passages.text: Therefore, neither are the Hebrews condemned for not knowing Jesus, because of the one who hid him, provided that, while doing the things through Moses .... they do not hate the one they did not know; nor, in turn, are those from the nations who did not know Moses condemned because of the one who concealed him, provided that they too, while doing the things spoken through Jesus, do not hate the one they did not know. Nor do people gain any benefit by calling their teachers “lords” while not performing servants’ duties. For this reason, our Jesus said to someone who repeatedly called him Lord but did nothing that he commanded: “Why do you call me ‘Lord, Lord,’ and not do what I say?” For saying will not benefit anyone, but doing will. In every way, therefore, good works are needed. Yet if anyone should be deemed worthy to recognize both of them as proclaiming one teaching, that man has been counted rich in God, having understood the ancient things to be new with respect to time and the new things to be old.

lexical_decisions.chosen: not performing servants’ duties
lexical_decisions.rationale: The substantival phrase means the things characteristic of servants; “servants’ duties” supplies natural English without weakening the status term.

lexical_decisions.chosen: repeatedly
lexical_decisions.rationale: The comparative adverb can mean “more frequently” or, idiomatically, “rather frequently”; the context emphasizes repeated address.

lexical_decisions.chosen: In every way, therefore
lexical_decisions.rationale: The idiom stresses necessity by every consideration; “by all means” is an alternative.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τά τε ἀρχαῖα νέα τῷ χρόνῳ καὶ τὰ καινὰ παλαιὰ ὄντα
lexical_decisions.chosen: the ancient things to be new with respect to time and the new things to be old
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering preserves the printed paradox. τῷ χρόνῳ may alternatively be understood as “with time” or “in relation to time.”

source_issues.source_quote: πράττοντες τὰ διὰ Μωϋσέως .... ὃν ἠγνόησαν μὴ μισήσωσιν
source_issues.issue: The supplied text contains a clearly printed four-dot gap after “the things through Moses.” Missing wording and its precise syntactic contribution cannot be recovered without invention, so the gap is retained.

passages.text: As Peter was saying these things, the crowds entered the place where he was, as though summoned by someone. When he saw the large crowd flowing gently in like the quiet current of a river, he said to Maroones, “Where around here do you have a place better able to hold the crowds?” When Maroones led him on to an outdoor place laid out as a garden, the crowds followed. Peter took his stand on the not very high pedestal of a statue and, immediately upon greeting the crowd according to a devout custom, knowing that many among the crowds present had for many years been tormented by demons and numerous afflictions, gnashing their teeth amid wailing and falling down in supplication, he rebuked them and ordered them to remain quiet. Then, after promising healing once he had delivered his discourse, he began to speak as follows:

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὥσπερ ποταμοῦ ἥσυχον ῥεῦμα πράως προσρέοντα
lexical_decisions.chosen: flowing gently in like the quiet current of a river
lexical_decisions.rationale: The comparison presents the approaching crowd as a calm river current rather than as a violent rush.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Maroones
lexical_decisions.rationale: The name is transliterated from its dative form; the corresponding nominative is Μαροόνης.

lexical_decisions.chosen: an outdoor place laid out as a garden
lexical_decisions.rationale: κεκηπευμένον describes a place cultivated or arranged as a garden; “a cultivated open-air place” is also possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: gnashing their teeth amid wailing
lexical_decisions.rationale: βρύχω commonly describes gnashing, though “roaring” or “growling” is lexically possible in this depiction.

lexical_decisions.chosen: once he had delivered his discourse
lexical_decisions.rationale: The passive-form verb is used in the deponent sense of speaking or discoursing; “after he had spoken” is a less specific alternative.

passages.text: As I begin to deliver the discourse concerning reverence for God to people who know nothing at all and whose minds have been stained by the slanders of Simon, our opponent, I have thought it necessary first to deliver a discourse on why one must not blame God, who made everything. I begin nowhere else than from the very occasion that he himself providentially presented at the opportune moment, so that it may be known that with good reason many people have been held fast by many demons and overtaken by strange afflictions, in order that in this too God’s justice may become apparent; and so that those who blame him through ignorance, even now, after learning how they ought to think, may call themselves back from their former accusation by speaking well and doing good, offering ignorance—the cause of their wicked audacity—as grounds for pardon.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὑπὸ τῶν τοῦ ἀντικειμένου ἡμῖν Σίμωνος διαβολῶν
lexical_decisions.chosen: by the slanders of Simon, our opponent
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive construction identifies Simon as the one opposing the speakers and as the source of the slanders.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἀπ᾽ αὐτῆς τῆς κατὰ πρόνοιαν ὑπ᾽ αὐτοῦ εὐκαίρως ὑποβληθείσης προφάσεως
lexical_decisions.chosen: from the very occasion that he himself providentially presented at the opportune moment
lexical_decisions.rationale: πρόφασις here can denote an occasion or starting point, not necessarily a deceptive pretext; αὐτοῦ most naturally refers to God, though the pronoun remains formally implicit in English.

lexical_decisions.chosen: with good reason
lexical_decisions.rationale: The adverb asserts that the demonic and physical afflictions occurred on reasonable or justifiable grounds, rather than merely describing them as intelligible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: may call themselves back from their former accusation
lexical_decisions.rationale: The wording can depict withdrawal from their prior accusation against God. Alternatively, ἔγκλημα may denote the charge or culpability they incurred, yielding “extricate themselves from their former charge.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: by speaking well and doing good
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering preserves the parallel between favorable speech and beneficial action; “through praise and good works” is also possible.

passages.text: The matter is as follows: when the only good God had made everything well and handed it over to the human being who had come into being according to his image, that created one, breathing the divinity of the one who made him, being a true prophet and knowing all things, in honor of the father who had given him everything and for the salvation of the sons who came from him, as a genuine father preserving his goodwill toward the children born from him, and wishing them, for their own benefit, to love God and be loved by him, revealed the road that leads to friendship with him. He taught by what human actions the sole God and Master of all rejoices; and, after declaring the things pleasing to him, he established an eternal law for all, one that cannot be burned up by war, secretly adulterated by any impious person, or hidden in a single place, but can be read by everyone. Consequently, through obedience to the law, everything was abundant for them: the finest fruits, the full span of years free from pain and disease, all securely bestowed along with every temperate condition of the air.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: παραδεδωκότος τῷ κατ᾽ εἰκόνα αὐτοῦ γενομένῳ ἀνθρώπῳ
lexical_decisions.chosen: handed it over to the human being who had come into being according to his image
lexical_decisions.rationale: παραδίδωμι here denotes handing over or entrusting the created order, while κατ᾽ εἰκόνα is retained as “according to his image.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῆς τοῦ πεποιηκότος αὐτὸν πνέων θειότητος
lexical_decisions.chosen: breathing the divinity of the one who made him
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive construction is preserved without resolving whether πνέων means breathing in, breathing forth, or manifesting the maker’s divinity.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὴν πρὸς φιλίαν αὐτοῦ ἄγουσαν ἐξέφηνεν ὁδόν
lexical_decisions.chosen: revealed the road that leads to friendship with him
lexical_decisions.rationale: αὐτοῦ most naturally refers to God; “his friendship” is possible but less explicit about the direction of the road.

lexical_decisions.chosen: he established an eternal law for all
lexical_decisions.rationale: τοῖς ὅλοις may refer to all people or to the whole created order; the inclusive “for all” preserves that breadth.

lexical_decisions.chosen: secretly adulterated by any impious person
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὑπονοθεύω denotes covert falsification, adulteration, or interpolation; “tampered with” is a broader alternative.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὰ τῶν ἐτῶν τέλεια καὶ ἄλυπα καὶ ἄνοσα
lexical_decisions.chosen: the full span of years free from pain and disease
lexical_decisions.rationale: The expression is elliptical; it can denote complete years or a full lifetime, characterized as painless and healthy.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: μετὰ πάσης τῆς τῶν ἀέρων εὐκρασίας
lexical_decisions.chosen: along with every temperate condition of the air
lexical_decisions.rationale: εὐκρασία denotes a favorable balance or temperateness, while the plural ἀέρων can encompass atmospheric or climatic conditions.

Translation Stance

This document states the translation commitments that guide every
decision in the People's Open Bible. Declaring them is an act of
honesty: critics can assess our output against our stated
commitments rather than guessing at hidden biases.

> **Status: first draft.** This document will be refined as the
> project matures. Input and disagreement are welcomed via GitHub
> issues.

## Theological stance

The People's Open Bible does not commit to a specific denominational
or creedal doctrinal stance. Where the source texts presuppose
theological claims — the divinity of Christ, the resurrection,
the personhood of the Holy Spirit, the unity of God — the
translation reflects those claims as the texts present them, not
as imposed commitments of the translator.

Readers from any tradition (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant
of any stripe, non-denominational, inquirer) are invited to
evaluate POB against their own framework. Where a translation
decision is influenced by a theological reading — for example,
where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

4. **Consistency of key terms, or documented exception.** A given
   Greek or Hebrew word should receive a consistent English gloss
   across the translation, unless context demands variance — in
   which case the variance is documented per-verse with a
   rationale. The `consistency_lint.py` tool enforces this at
   commit time.

5. **Readable modern English, not archaic or academic.** The
   target reader is a literate 18–35-year-old English speaker.
   Vocabulary should be accessible without flattening theological
   weight. We avoid both ecclesiastical jargon ("propitiation" is
   footnoted, not required) and informality that undersells the
   text's gravity.

## Source distinctions and optimal English

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for
maintainer review; do not silently certify them as unchanged or auto-publish.

**Approved scoped rendering:** John 21:15–17 uses **agape-love** for ἀγαπάω
and **phileo-love** for φιλέω, including the repeated question in verse 17.
The ἀγάπη noun's general table entry below is not a rule erasing that verb
pattern. Do not revert this approved POB/SPOB wording to generic “love”.

## Contested terms

The following terms appear frequently and carry heavy theological
weight. Our default rendering and rationale are recorded here.
Per-verse variance is documented in the individual YAML files.

| Greek / Hebrew | Default English | Alternatives considered | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| Χριστός *Christos* | Messiah where independently titular; Christ in the name forms "Jesus Christ" / "Christ Jesus" | Christ, Messiah | Preserves the title's Hebraic messianic meaning while using the recognizable conventional English personal name |
| κύριος *Kyrios* | Lord | LORD, Master | Matches covenantal and NT usage |
| δοῦλος *doulos* | servant | bondservant, slave | Uses reader-facing "servant" consistently; documents bonded-status and ownership nuance in notes/audit metadata |
| πίστις *pistis* | faith | faithfulness, trust | Main text: faith; footnote alternatives where contested |
| δικαιοσύνη *dikaiosynē* | righteousness | justice | Both renderings preserved in footnotes for Pauline passages |
| ἱλαστήριον *hilastērion* | atoning sacrifice | propitiation, mercy seat | Dynamic rendering for accessibility; alternatives footnoted |
| ἀγάπη *agapē* | love | charity (archaic) | Lexical cognates in source kept |
| σάρξ *sarx* | flesh (literal) / sinful nature (metaphorical) | — | Context-dependent; per-verse documented |
| μετανοέω / μετάνοια *metanoeō / metanoia* | reorient / reorientation; toward God where the context warrants making the destination explicit | repent / repentance (traditional); reconsider / change of mind in documented exceptions | See "Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)" below; do not homogenize regret, divine relenting, or distinct turning words |
| νήφω *nēphō* | clear-minded (most contexts); sober (where Paul explicitly runs the drunk/sober metaphor) | sober-minded | See revision notes in 1 Pet 5:8, 1 Thess 5:6 |

| אָדָם *adam* | man / humankind (context) | — | Context-dependent per usage |

## Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)

Maintainer-approved English POB and SPOB reader wording uses **reorient /
reorientation** in place of the repent family for moral-spiritual redirection.
Use **toward God** when the context warrants making that direction explicit;
use **toward you** in direct prayer, and omit the extra destination when the
sentence already names it, supplies a departure from wrongdoing, or concerns
interpersonal reconsideration. Acts 20:21 explicitly supplies the Godward
phrase. The word *metanoia* by itself does not lexically contain "God."

This is an English editorial policy, not a claim that remorse is irrelevant or
that Greek word parts establish the full meaning. Preserve sorrow, named sins,
faith, forgiveness, and the distinction between a response and its fruit.
Keep separate turning expressions in Acts 3:19 and 26:20. Baptism's relationship
to reorientation must not be rewritten as "only symbolizes" or "causes."

**Context controls exceptions.** Retain regret, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where that is the supported sense. Do not make
God reorient toward God; do not make a persecutor's demand for apostasy a call
toward God. Preserve contested interpretations in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17.
Extra-canonical authors retain their own conceptual frameworks. Adapting a
historical English witness is not a new ancient-language translation, and must
be disclosed while its source transcription remains untouched.

**No invented intensifiers.** Do not add "fully," "completely," "radically,"
"truly," "wholeheartedly," or a superlative simply to strengthen reorientation.
Preserve such force only where the source supplies it. Hermas V.3.xiii.4
(reader chapter 21:4) has *holotelōs* and *ex holēs kardias*; its existing
"completely" and "from their whole heart" are not new additions.

Traditional terminology remains in alternative notes, original sources, and
historical revision records. Do not rewrite those layers to manufacture a
history of agreement. See [the application report](docs/REORIENTATION_POLICY_2026-10-11.md)
and the hash-bound plan in `config/terminology/`.

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.
- **Not a study Bible.** Footnotes document translation decisions,
  not doctrinal application or devotional commentary.
- **Not a denominational product.** The translation is
  intentionally cross-denominational. Contested readings are
  preserved in footnotes, not smoothed away.
- **Not a finalized translation.** Every verse is currently an
  AI-drafted rendering, released openly with full rationale. There
  is no formal scholarly review process at this time.
- **Not a first-century English approximation.** We aim at modern
  English that honors source-language meaning, not at archaism.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model
performance and feasibility.** Not every language has an AI model
capable of scholarly-accurate translation yet, and not every
language has a sufficient community of native-speaking reviewers
accessible to the project. We will publish the current supported-
language list, and the ready-but-not-yet-stable list, as we reach
the capability threshold for each. Languages that do not yet meet
the bar are named as such, not silently omitted.

Every language published under this program carries the same
CC-BY 4.0 license, the same per-verse provenance, the same
auditability. There is no tier system across languages — every
supported language gets the full People's Open Bible.
